Field studies of the Andean hairy armadillo (Chaetophractus nationi) have begun to clarify its life-history strategy, which appears to be shaped by the cold, seasonal conditions of the high-altitude Altiplano. Under standard laboratory conditions maintained at a stable core temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], direct respirometry on post-absorptive adults has revealed a basal metabolic rate of 559.00 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 559.00 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This relatively modest metabolic expenditure, characteristic of small edentates with low thermal conductance, corresponds to the maximum basal oxygen consumption recorded for the species under resting conditions. The acquisition of this parameter is critical for constructing accurate energetic models, as it represents the minimal energetic cost of maintaining homeostasis under thermoneutral conditions.

Reproductive effort in this xeric-adapted xenarthran is notably constrained. Females produce a single annual litter [F_R_i = single annual litter], with the average litter comprising exactly two pups [N_R_i = litter comprising exactly two pups], resulting in a maximum yearly reproductive output of just two offspring per adult female. This low fecundity is consistent with a slow life-history pace common among armadillos. The timing of these events is closely tied to the brief austral summer, when resource availability peaks at the elevated ambient temperatures typical of the active season. When the maternal body is experimentally maintained at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], this annual schedule yields a calculated reproductive output of 2 pups per 365 days [Ri = 2 pups per 365 days], underscoring the notably restricted reproductive potential of this species relative to similarly sized mammals from less seasonal environments.

Neonatal characteristics reflect the substantial maternal investment required to produce a single pair of precocial offspring. Newborn individuals, examined within 24 hours of parturition, exhibit a mean wet body mass of 81.3 grams [Wwb = 81.3 grams], a value estimated by scaling from the closely related Chaetophractus villosus. This substantial birth mass, representing approximately 3.8 percent of the adult female's ultimate body weight, is indicative of an extended gestation period that allows for significant in utero development. In contrast, the ultimate wet body mass attained by adult females reaches an average of 2150 grams [Wwi = 2150 grams], a figure that stabilizes after the completion of skeletal growth and represents the asymptotic size class for reproductive females in natural populations.

Longevity records for this species, derived from both mark-recapture programs in the Bolivian altiplano and captive-rearing studies conducted at a stable core temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years], placing Chaetophractus nationi among the longest-lived of all xenarthrans relative to its body mass. This exceptional longevity, when expressed in daily terms, amounts to roughly 7300 days [am = roughly 7300 days] under consistent thermal co at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]nditions. The gestational investment that underpins this slow life history includes a gestation period lasting 60 consecutive days (60 days) [tg = 60 days], a relatively extended intrauterine development that permits the delivery of fully formed, partially ossified young capable of independent locomotion shortly after birth at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C].

Post-natal development proceeds through a tightly scheduled sequence of milestones under the thermoneutral conditions of 35.5 °C typical of this species' active physiology. The age at weaning, defined as the cessation of maternal lactation, occurs at 50 days after birth [tx = 50 days after birth], a point at which juveniles begin to subsist entirely on solid insect prey at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. The weaned young then enter a prolonged sub-adult phase lasting approximately 9 months, culminating in the onset of sexual maturity at 274.5 days after birth [tp = 274.5 days after birth] at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This significant delay in pubertal development, equivalent to roughly nine 30.5-day lunar months, reflects the extended period of skeletal and physiological maturation required before females can successfully support the energetic demands of gestation and lactation in the harsh, resource-poor environment of the high Andes.
